::: {.kw-overview}
Two large US registry analyses this week examine donor characteristics that current allocation schemes weight poorly or not at all. In more than 155,000 transplants, a small donor relative to the recipient, expressed as the body-surface-area ratio, was second only to donor age as a predictor of one-year graft function, while a separate analysis of 136,000 recipients found that one-year rejection rose progressively with donor age, with the youngest paediatric donors carrying the lowest risk. European registry data on more than 12,000 patients who started kidney replacement therapy in childhood confirm that pre-emptive and living-donor transplantation, together with a durable first graft, give the best long-term graft survival, including after re-transplantation. In perioperative care, a Bayesian meta-analysis found that quadratus lumborum and transversus abdominis plane blocks reduce opioid requirements but that the evidence is of very low certainty, and a systematic review of infected transplant arterial complications favours autologous interposition grafting over ligation or primary repair. On infection, a review of adoptive BK polyomavirus-specific T-cell therapy reports consistent virological responses without demonstrated recovery of graft function. Finally, a two-cohort study links ADPKD to excess venous thromboembolism after transplantation, partly through higher haemoglobin, and a European position paper proposes an individualised, ultrasound- and cardiology-guided approach to the arteriovenous fistula after transplantation.
:::

---

### 1. [Donor-Recipient Size Mismatch is a Critical Determinant of Kidney Transplant Outcome.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ekir.2026.107100)
[Amarnath DR, Kourounis G, Glover EK, Akhtar MZ, Sheerin NS, Wilson CH, Tingle SJ. *Kidney Int Rep*, 2026. PMID: 42936386.]{.kw-ref}

This Newcastle-led analysis of US OPTN registry data examined whether a mismatch between donor nephron supply and recipient demand, represented by the ratio of donor to recipient body surface area, influences outcome. It included adult deceased-donor kidney-only transplants performed between 2010 and mid-2024, excluding retransplants and en bloc paediatric kidneys, and modelled the ratio as a continuous variable using restricted cubic splines with adjustment for donor size itself. Among 155,438 single-kidney transplants, kidneys from donors smaller than their recipients performed consistently worse. With other factors held constant, a ratio at the 5th percentile (0.76) compared with the 95th (1.37) corresponded to a predicted one-year eGFR of 50.7 versus 71.2 mL/min/1.73 m², a difference of 20.5 (95% CI 19.9 to 21.1), and to an almost twofold hazard of graft loss at five years (adjusted HR 1.93, 95% CI 1.75 to 2.13). In the full text, each 0.1 increase in the ratio was associated with an eGFR gain of approximately 3.2 mL/min/1.73 m², and the ratio was also associated with delayed graft function. Of 36 factors examined, only donor age was more strongly associated with one-year eGFR, and the ratio outranked several variables used in UK, US and European offering schemes, including HLA mismatch and waiting time. The effect did not vary in a clinically meaningful way with donor age or donor–recipient sex combination, and a ratio based on ideal donor body weight performed best as a single stand-alone metric. The authors note that body surface area is an imperfect surrogate for nephron mass and that the design is retrospective; they provide a free online calculator. Because the authors note that most current offering schemes and risk indices overlook size mismatch, the study supports evaluating size matching in future allocation revisions of the UK scheme and accounting for it as a confounder in observational and trial analyses.

### 2. [Born to Be Accepted: Donor age Association With One-year Rejection in Deceased Donor Kidney Transplants.](https://doi.org/10.1097/TXD.0000000000002020)
[Herrera NS, Ramakrishnan M, Ahrens ML, Schmitt N, Cibrik DM. *Transplant Direct*, 2026. PMID: 42923909.]{.kw-ref}

Concern about rejection is one reason kidneys from paediatric donors are underused, and this study tested that concern using Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients data for first-time adult deceased-donor recipients transplanted between 2014 and 2025. Any reported acute rejection within 12 months was modelled with center-clustered logistic regression using only pre-transplant covariates, and donor age was divided into five groups at data-derived cut-points. Of 136,182 recipients, 8,803 (6.5%) had a rejection episode. Recipients of kidneys from donors younger than 3.5 years had an unadjusted rejection rate of 4.8%, compared with 6.5% for all older donors. After adjustment, the odds of rejection increased stepwise across older donor groups, from an odds ratio of 1.59 (95% CI 1.25 to 2.04) for donors aged 3.5 to 18.3 years to 2.49 (95% CI 1.88 to 3.28) for donors older than 61.3 years, and the standardised probability of rejection rose from 3.9% to 9.1%. En bloc kidneys differed significantly from all older groups, whereas non-en bloc kidneys from the youngest donors differed only from the two oldest groups. The age cut-points were derived post hoc, and registry reporting of rejection may be incomplete. For UK centres, the data suggest that fear of rejection should not count against accepting kidneys from very young donors.

### 3. [Long-term patient and graft survival for children and young adults after kidney transplantation and re-transplantation - results from the ERA Registry.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2026.10.017)
[Preka E, Bonthuis M, Marks SD, Kramer A, Stel VS, Buchwinkler L, Ponte B, Åsberg A, Stabouli S, Stojanovic J, Sørensen SS, Gjerstad AC, Herrero-Goñi M, Rodriguez Arévalo OL, Tsimaratos M, Kuzema V, Segelmark M, Palsson R, Ortiz A, Jager KJ, Harambat J. *Am J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42951115.]{.kw-ref}

This descriptive European Renal Association Registry study followed 12,623 patients who began kidney replacement therapy before the age of 20 and received a first (11,078), second (2,962) or third (718) kidney transplant between 1978 and 2019. Patient survival remained high regardless of transplant number: at 15 years it was 90% after a first, 94% after a second and 92% after a third transplant. Graft survival declined with each successive transplant, from 79%, 63% and 50% at 5, 10 and 15 years after a first transplant to 67%, 51% and 38% after a third. After a first transplant, pre-emptive transplantation was associated with lower mortality (adjusted HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.80) and lower graft failure (0.89, 0.82 to 0.97), as was living donation (mortality 0.71, 0.61 to 0.83; graft failure 0.76, 0.70 to 0.81). Graft failure risk was higher between the ages of 10 and 24 years, in females, and in patients with glomerulonephritis, metabolic disease or a recurrent primary disease. For second and subsequent transplants, living-donor and pre-emptive grafts and a previous graft that had functioned for more than five years were associated with better graft survival. The study is descriptive and spans four decades of practice. For UK paediatric and transition services, the findings support prioritising pre-emptive living donation and give realistic survival figures for counselling young people who face a second or third transplant.

### 4. [Regional analgesic techniques for postoperative pain after kidney transplantation: a systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2026.09.018)
[Azem K, Ofir AY, Heesen P, Ronen A, Khinchuk A, Kanani F, Mansour Y, Nesher E, Arzola C, Fein S, Aranbitski R. *Br J Anaesth*, 2026. PMID: 42946571.]{.kw-ref}

Earlier syntheses of regional analgesia in transplantation pooled different blocks together, mixed donors with recipients and did not use a clinically meaningful threshold. This registered review searched PubMed, Embase and CENTRAL up to 5 September 2026 for randomised trials in adult kidney recipients and used Bayesian random-effects models with priors scaled to minimal clinically important differences, with certainty assessed by GRADE. Fourteen trials involving 903 participants were included, but only the quadratus lumborum and transversus abdominis plane blocks had enough data to be pooled against control. Both lowered pain scores at every time point, but no comparison had at least an 80% probability of exceeding the 1-point clinically important difference. The opioid-sparing effect at 24 hours was more convincing: quadratus lumborum blocks reduced consumption by 15.5 morphine milligram equivalents (95% credible interval −23.6 to −6.7) and transversus abdominis plane blocks by 10.5 (−14.4 to −5.5), each with a greater than 97% probability of exceeding the 5 mg threshold. A network analysis found no meaningful difference between the two blocks. Data on graft function and safety were too sparse to pool, 12 registered trials remained unpublished, and overall certainty was very low. For UK units, either block is a reasonable opioid-sparing adjunct, but the evidence does not favour one technique over the other or establish any effect on graft function.

### 5. [Vascular Management Strategies and Outcomes of Infectious Arterial Complications Involving the Kidney Transplant Vasculature: A Systematic Review and Evidence-Informed Treatment Framework.](https://doi.org/10.1111/ctr.70734)
[Mozafar M, Bigdeli Y, Lichani MA, Looha MA, Mozafar M, Modarai B, Lyon O, Yi S, Kagan A, Grimes KA, Rahimi M. *Clin Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42945230.]{.kw-ref}

Infection of the transplant renal artery, iliac vessels or anastomosis is rare but often results in graft loss, and there is no evidence-based guidance on its vascular management. This review searched from database inception to August 2025 for culture-proven cases of rupture, pseudoaneurysm, aneurysm, thrombosis or stenosis, and because the evidence was heterogeneous it compared outcomes descriptively by proportion. Eighty reports published between 1972 and 2025 described 139 cases. Candida was the most frequent pathogen, followed by Pseudomonas, Aspergillus and Staphylococcus, and most cases presented as pseudoaneurysm or rupture within the first month. Outcomes were generally better when the graft was preserved. Autologous interposition grafting had the best record, with 86.7% uneventful recovery and 6.7% reintervention and mortality, including in patients who required transplant nephrectomy. Covered stents were the most commonly reported intervention and achieved uneventful recovery in 75% of selected graft-preserving cases. Primary repair had the highest reintervention rate (59.1%), and arterial ligation had the highest mortality (43.8%) and accounted for every reported limb loss. The evidence comes from case reports and small series spanning five decades, so the authors present it as guidance rather than a protocol. For UK transplant surgeons, the review supports autologous reconstruction where possible, with stenting reserved for selected cases or temporary haemorrhage control, and its findings indicate that ligation carries the greatest risk.

### 6. [Efficacy and Safety of Adoptive BK Polyomavirus-Reactive T-Cell Therapy for Active Infection or Disease in Transplant Recipients: A Systematic Review.](https://doi.org/10.3390/v18101166)
[Bratosin F, Kodimala SC, Croitor A, Dema V, Rosca O. *Viruses*, 2026. PMID: 42944085.]{.kw-ref}

No antiviral has proven efficacy against BK polyomavirus, and this review assessed adoptively transferred BK-specific T cells used to treat active infection after haematopoietic cell or kidney transplantation. PubMed, Europe PMC and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched to 1 September 2026, prophylaxis-only reports were excluded, and the review followed PRISMA 2020 and SWiM guidance, linking overlapping publications rather than counting them twice. Twenty-two reports were included, with 15 independent cohorts contributing 241 evaluable recipients. Overall, 178 (73.9%) responded according to each study's own definition, and the pooled response proportion was 87% (95% CI 73 to 97), with substantial heterogeneity (I² 70%). Response rates were similar for cystitis, DNAemia and nephropathy, but no cohort showed consistent recovery of kidney function once nephropathy was established, in contrast to the resolution of haematuria in 19 of 25 patients with cystitis. In the only placebo-controlled kidney trial, more posoleucel recipients than placebo recipients achieved a decline in viral load by week 24; however, three placebo-controlled posoleucel trials after haematopoietic cell transplantation were stopped in December 2023 for futility. Rejection was reported in 4 of 69 (5.8%) treated kidney recipients and in none of 19 on placebo, and one death from cytokine release syndrome occurred. Most of the evidence is uncontrolled and overlapping, and comparative benefit for graft outcome has not been shown. For UK kidney teams, the therapy remains investigational, and the authors suggest that future trials target persistent DNAemia after reduction of immunosuppression has failed, before fibrosis is established.

### 7. [Risk of Venous Thromboembolism in Kidney Transplant Recipients with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease.](https://doi.org/10.1681/ASN.0000001298)
[Bais T, Alnaim AA, Tegzess E, Binet I, Dickenmann M, Golshayan D, Haidar F, Kuhn C, Schachtner T, Hübel K, Meijer K, Eisenga MF, Sanders JS, Berger SP, Gansevoort RT, Sidler D, Bocchi F. *J Am Soc Nephrol*, 2026. PMID: 42931822.]{.kw-ref}

This observational study compared venous thromboembolism after transplantation in recipients with and without ADPKD at a Dutch centre (Groningen; 1,179 recipients, 393 with ADPKD) and repeated the key analyses in the multicentre Swiss Transplant Cohort Study (4,415 recipients, 710 with ADPKD). Thromboembolism was more common in ADPKD in both cohorts. The 10-year cumulative incidence was 13.5% versus 9.6% in Groningen and 21.0% versus 15.1% in the Swiss cohort. Events clustered in the first two years, with a median time to thromboembolism of about one and a half years in both cohorts. After adjustment for established risk factors, ADPKD remained independently associated with thromboembolism (HR 1.80, 95% CI 1.21 to 2.69 in Groningen; 1.39, 1.13 to 1.72 in Switzerland), and the association was stronger in men. Post-transplant haemoglobin was about 7% higher in ADPKD recipients, particularly men, who also developed erythrocytosis more often; including haemoglobin as a time-varying covariate weakened the association, which suggests that it partly explains the excess risk. As an observational study, it cannot show that lowering haemoglobin would reduce thrombosis. For UK clinics, the findings justify closer monitoring for post-transplant erythrocytosis in ADPKD recipients, especially men, and greater attention to thromboembolism risk in the first two years after transplantation.

### 8. [Vascular access management after kidney transplantation position paper on behalf of the Vascular Access Society and the European Kidney Transplant Association.](https://doi.org/10.1177/11297298261468406)
[Akin B, Jemcov TK, Cucchiari D, Malik J, Pettigrew GJ, Hahn Lundström U, Zaza G, Rotmans JI. *J Vasc Access*, 2026. PMID: 42908338.]{.kw-ref}

International guidelines do not address whether an uncomplicated arteriovenous fistula should be ligated or preserved after a successful transplant, and this joint position paper from the Vascular Access Society and the European Kidney Transplant Association aims to fill that gap. The authors point out that as graft survival improves, recipients are exposed for longer to the haemodynamic load of a functioning fistula. Ligation reduces left ventricular mass, but its effect on cardiovascular events or mortality is not known. High-flow access causes complications in some recipients, and immunosuppression may increase the risk. The paper also notes that a preserved fistula often goes unused: central venous catheters are used in nearly two-thirds of patients who return to haemodialysis. The authors therefore recommend an individualised, multidisciplinary decision guided by an algorithm that combines Doppler ultrasound with cardiac assessment, taking into account the possibility of ligation followed by reconstruction if dialysis becomes necessary again. The abstract describes the recommendations only in outline and gives no outcome data. In the absence of consensus, the paper gives UK units a framework for a structured, documented review of the fistula after transplantation in place of either routine ligation or indefinite preservation.
